1.title: Sleep and the Teenage Body Clock

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts. Research since the 1990s has shown that teenagers produce the sleep hormone melatonin about two hours later than children or adults do, which makes it hard for them to fall asleep before 11 p.m. Yet most secondary schools begin lessons before 8.30 a.m., so many students must get up at a time when their bodies are still biologically 'at night'.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The consequences have been measured in several studies. A survey of 9,000 students found that those who slept fewer than seven hours were 30 per cent more likely to report low mood and almost twice as likely to fall asleep in class. Teachers also noticed that attention and short-term memory were weakest in the first lesson of the day. Some researchers argue that the effect on exam results is smaller than the effect on mood, but all of them agree that chronic sleep loss is not harmless.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Several school districts have tried to respond by delaying the start of the school day. In one trial involving five schools, the start time was moved from 7.30 to 8.45. After two years, attendance had risen by 5 per cent and the number of late arrivals had fallen by nearly a quarter, and reports of low mood had dropped by 12 per cent. Interestingly, students did not go to bed later than before, which means that they gained roughly an extra hour of sleep each night.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics, however, point to practical difficulties. Later starts mean later finishes, which can clash with sports practice, part-time jobs and the working hours of parents who rely on the school day to organise childcare. Bus timetables must also be rewritten, and in rural areas this may increase costs. Some educators therefore favour smaller changes, such as teaching the most demanding subjects later in the morning, while others suggest that families should limit evening screen use, since the blue light from devices can delay melatonin even further.

paragraphs.text: Roughly one in seven children in many urban areas of Western Europe now grows up in a household where the parents were born abroad. Sociologists often call them 'second-generation' citizens, a label that suggests a straightforward story of adaptation. Recent research, however, paints a more complicated picture, in which young people move continually between two sets of expectations about language, food, religion and family duty.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Language is the clearest example. In a study of 400 teenagers, most reported that they spoke their parents' language at home but switched to the national language with friends and at school. In figures, 72 per cent used their parents' language at home, while 88 per cent used the national language with friends. Around 45 per cent said that their command of their heritage language, particularly in writing, was weaker than their parents would have liked. Linguists call this pattern language shift, and by the third generation the heritage language has often disappeared altogether.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Identity proved to be just as flexible. Rather than choosing one culture over the other, many participants described a 'situational' identity, emphasising different aspects of their background depending on the audience. Some reported feeling like outsiders in both communities, while others said that the ability to see a situation from two perspectives made them better negotiators and more tolerant of difference.

paragraphs.label: D

Parents who had left their country for economic reasons often hoped that their children would study law or medicine, and many young people felt a strong obligation to repay their parents' sacrifices. The researchers found that the teenagers who coped best were neither those who obeyed nor those who rebelled, but those who negotiated: they explained their own goals calmly and looked for a compromise.

paragraphs.label: E

All of the participants lived in the same large city, where cultural diversity is highly visible and community organisations are well funded. paragraphs.text: Many people believe that children learn languages far better than adults, and there is some truth in this. Children who are exposed to a new language before the age of ten usually acquire a pronunciation that is almost indistinguishable from that of native speakers. paragraphs.text: Every wave of new technology has provoked fears of mass unemployment. In the early nineteenth century, textile workers destroyed mechanical looms that threatened their livelihoods, and in the twentieth century the arrival of computers prompted similar anxiety. paragraphs.text: Predictions about the scale of the threat diverge sharply. One analysis of 700 occupations concluded that nearly half were at high risk of automation within two decades. A later study criticised this method on the grounds that it treated whole occupations as single units, whereas most jobs contain a mixture of routine and non-routine activities. paragraphs.label: D

Workers who lose routine manufacturing jobs seldom move directly into the new technology roles, and entire regions can suffer long periods of high unemployment. 4.title: Working from Home: A Technological Shift

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Before 2020, fewer than one in ten employees in most developed countries worked from home on a regular basis. Within a few weeks of the first lockdowns, however, millions of people were logging in from kitchens and spare bedrooms. Video calling software, cloud storage and online project boards made this change possible, and many companies discovered that their staff could carry out much of their work without ever entering an office.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The benefits soon became clear. A survey of 2,000 employees found that the average worker saved fifty-four minutes a day by not commuting, and most of them used part of that time to sleep or exercise. Employers also noticed savings: one engineering firm reduced its office space by a third and spent the money on training courses instead. Some managers reported that their staff were more productive at home because there were fewer interruptions from colleagues.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone was convinced, though. Workers who lived alone often said that they felt isolated, and younger employees complained that they missed the informal advice that colleagues share in corridors and kitchens. If a new recruit never meets the team in person, one manager argued, it is difficult to build trust. There were also practical problems. Around one in six people in the same survey did not have a quiet place to work, and some had to use a dining table that was shared with children.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Today, many organisations have settled on a hybrid model, in which staff spend two or three days in the office and the rest at home. Researchers who followed 500 workers over a year found that this arrangement led to the lowest rate of resignation. Annual resignation was 7 per cent among hybrid workers, 11 per cent among those who were always in the office and 14 per cent among those who were always at home. However, they also warned that hybrid work can be unfair. Employees who come to the office more often may be noticed by senior managers and promoted sooner than those who stay at home. 4.title: Algorithms and the Future of Work

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The idea that machines might replace human workers is not new. In the early nineteenth century, textile workers in England smashed mechanical looms because they feared for their livelihoods. Yet over the following century, employment in industrial economies grew rather than shrank, as new industries absorbed those who had lost their jobs. Many economists draw comfort from this history, arguing that technology destroys particular tasks but creates demand for others.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Others are less optimistic. They observe that modern algorithms are different in kind from earlier machinery, because they can perform cognitive tasks such as reading medical scans, drafting legal contracts or assessing loan applications. A widely discussed estimate suggested that nearly half of existing occupations in one large economy were at high risk of automation within two decades. Critics of that figure, however, note that it measured technical possibility, not what employers would actually choose to do; a job may be automatable yet remain cheaper to leave in human hands.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A more recent analysis shifts the focus from whole jobs to individual tasks. Examining 800 occupations, the researchers concluded that fewer than five per cent could be entirely automated with current technology, whereas around 60 per cent contained at least a third of tasks that could be. In the study, about 40 per cent of occupations had fewer than a third of their tasks open to automation. The likely result, they argued, is not mass unemployment but the redesign of work. Accountants, for instance, may spend less time on routine calculations and more on advising clients, a change that rewards interpersonal skills.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even so, the transition will not be painless. Workers displaced by automation are often older, with skills that do not transfer easily, and retraining programmes have a mixed record. Studies of such schemes in several countries found that participants were only modestly more likely to find employment than similar people who received no help. Moreover, the gains from productivity tend to flow to the owners of capital and to highly educated workers, which may deepen inequality unless governments intervene through taxation or education policy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The debate therefore turns less on whether technology will change the labour market, which is certain, than on who will bear the cost. Policymakers who treat displacement as a temporary inconvenience may underestimate the difficulties facing individuals, while those who predict widespread joblessness risk discouraging investment in the very skills that workers will need.

4.title: Privacy in the Age of Big Data

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every time a person searches the web, uses a loyalty card or walks past a camera linked to a facial recognition system, a small record is created. Individually, these records seem harmless. Collected together, however, they allow companies and governments to infer a startling amount about a person's habits, health and political views. The accumulation of such information, often described as big data, has prompted fierce debate about where the boundary between convenience and intrusion should be drawn.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Defenders of data collection stress its benefits. Hospitals analyse anonymous records to identify which treatments work best for particular groups of patients, and city councils use mobile phone signals to redesign bus routes. Retailers argue that personalised recommendations save customers time. According to one industry survey, 70 per cent of consumers said they would share personal details in return for a lower price, suggesting that many people regard privacy as a commodity that can be traded.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Privacy campaigners dispute this interpretation. They point out that people rarely read the lengthy terms and conditions they accept, so consent is often more apparent than real. In one survey, only 9 per cent of respondents said they always read the terms in full, 31 per cent said they sometimes did, and 60 per cent said they never did. In one experiment, researchers designed a fictitious application whose terms stated that users' photographs could be sold to advertisers; 94 per cent of 200 volunteers accepted without hesitation. Furthermore, supposedly anonymous data can often be re-identified when it is combined with other sources. In one dataset, a combination of postcode, date of birth and gender was sufficient to identify most individuals.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Legislation has begun to respond. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, introduced in 2018, requires organisations to explain clearly why they collect data and gives individuals the right to have it deleted. Fines can reach four per cent of a company's global annual turnover, a sum large enough to change corporate behaviour. Other countries have since drafted similar laws, though enforcement varies considerably, and some critics claim that smaller firms struggle with the administrative burden of compliance more than large technology companies do.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Yet regulation alone may not resolve the underlying tension. Some scholars argue that the real issue is not secrecy but power: individuals know little about how their data are used, while organisations know a great deal about individuals. Until that imbalance is addressed, through clearer disclosure and independent audits, for example, public trust is likely to remain fragile, and the benefits of data-driven services may be undermined by the suspicion they provoke.

paragraphs.text: Most doctors recommend that teenagers sleep for between eight and ten hours each night, yet surveys suggest that fewer than a third actually do so. During adolescence the body's internal clock shifts, which makes young people feel sleepy later in the evening and want to wake later in the morning. paragraphs.text: In the past decade, more than forty countries and cities have introduced taxes on sugary drinks. The aim is straightforward: if a bottle of fizzy drink becomes more expensive, people will buy less of it, and consumption of sugar, which contributes to obesity and tooth decay, will fall. Second, some consumers simply switch to cheaper brands or travel to neighbouring areas where prices are lower; one study found that shoppers living near the border of a taxed city bought so many soft drinks outside it that almost half of the expected decline was cancelled out. Third, drinks are only one source of sugar, and people may compensate by eating more sweets or biscuits.

They add that the benefits are likely to build up over time. The study projected that the number of cases prevented would grow steadily, from about 10,000 after two years to 30,000 after four, 60,000 after six, 80,000 after eight and 100,000 after ten.

paragraphs.text: For decades, public health campaigns focused on diet, exercise and smoking. More recently, researchers have begun to draw attention to a less visible threat: loneliness. A widely cited analysis, which combined the results of dozens of studies, concluded that people with strong social relationships were around 50 per cent more likely to survive over a given period than those with weak ones, an effect comparable to that of giving up smoking.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: It is important to distinguish loneliness from social isolation. The latter is an objective condition, measured by the number of contacts a person has, while loneliness is a subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. A retired person who lives alone but speaks to friends daily may not feel lonely at all, whereas a young professional in a crowded office may feel deeply so. In one national survey, 10 per cent of adults aged 16 to 24 said they often felt lonely, compared with 7 per cent of those aged 25 to 44, 6 per cent of those aged 45 to 64 and 8 per cent of those aged 65 and over. Some studies suggest that the subjective feeling carries the greater health risk, although others find that isolation is the stronger predictor of early death.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the link. Chronic loneliness appears to raise levels of the stress hormone cortisol, which, over time, can contribute to high blood pressure and weaken the immune system. Lonely individuals also tend to sleep badly and to take less exercise, partly because they have no companions to motivate them. A further possibility is that causation runs in the opposite direction: people who are already unwell may withdraw from social life, so that poor health produces loneliness rather than the reverse.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Interventions have had uneven results. Programmes that simply bring older people together for tea and conversation rarely produce lasting benefits. By contrast, schemes that give participants a purpose, such as volunteering or teaching a skill, seem more effective. One trial in which retired adults helped children learn to read reported improvements in both mood and physical activity after six months. Evaluators caution, however, that the sample was small and that participants chose to take part, so more motivated individuals may have been over-represented.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whatever the precise mechanism, some governments now treat loneliness as a policy issue. One country has appointed a minister with responsibility for the subject, and doctors in several regions can prescribe community activities such as walking groups or art classes. 5.title: Why Good Intentions Fail: The Science of Habit

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Each January, millions of people resolve to exercise more, eat better or give up smoking. By February, a large proportion have abandoned their plans. One widely quoted study of 3,000 resolution-makers found that only 46 per cent were still keeping their resolutions after six months. This is a higher figure than many expected, yet it still means that more than half had given up. Psychologists have long sought to explain why good intentions so often collapse.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A common explanation is that willpower is a limited resource. According to this view, every decision, from choosing a meal to resisting a biscuit, draws on the same mental energy, so that by evening people are less able to resist temptation. However, attempts to reproduce the original experiments have produced inconsistent results, and many researchers now doubt that willpower works like a fuel tank. Instead, they emphasise the role of beliefs: individuals who think of willpower as unlimited appear to cope better with demanding tasks than those who think it runs out.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: An alternative approach concentrates on habits rather than motivation. A habit is a behaviour that has become automatic because it is repeatedly performed in the same context, such as brushing teeth after breakfast. One laboratory study estimated that forming a new habit took about two months on average, although the range was enormous, from less than three weeks to more than eight months, depending on the person and the behaviour. Simple actions, such as drinking a glass of water at lunch, became automatic far sooner than complex ones, such as completing fifty sit-ups. In the study, drinking a glass of water became automatic after about 20 days, compared with 66 days for all behaviours combined and about 120 days for fifty sit-ups.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Habit researchers therefore recommend making the desired behaviour as easy as possible. Placing running shoes beside the bed, for example, reduces the effort needed to start. They also suggest linking a new behaviour to an existing routine, a technique known as habit stacking. By contrast, setting vague goals such as getting fit tends to be ineffective, because it does not specify when, where or how the behaviour will occur. Studies of implementation intentions, in which people write down exactly what they will do in a given situation, show that this simple step can double the likelihood of success.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even so, no technique guarantees success. Social circumstances, work pressures and illness all disrupt routines, and a single missed day is often interpreted as total failure. Researchers observe that missing one occasion does not significantly damage progress, provided that people return to the routine quickly. The most useful lesson may therefore be a modest one: consistency matters more than perfection.

6.title: Coral Reefs in a Warming Ocean

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. They also protect coastlines from storms and provide food and income for roughly half a billion people. Because reef-building corals live close to the upper limit of the temperatures they can tolerate, they are among the first ecosystems to be affected by climate change.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: When the sea becomes too warm, corals expel the microscopic algae that live in their tissue and provide them with most of their energy. The coral then turns white, a process known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is weakened, and if the high temperatures continue for more than a few weeks, it may starve. Between 2014 and 2017, an unusually long marine heatwave caused bleaching on reefs in all three major ocean basins, and on one famous reef system about half of the shallow-water corals died. Surveys of that reef system recorded live coral cover falling to 85 per cent of its 2014 level in 2015, 60 per cent in 2016 and 50 per cent in 2017.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Warming is not the only danger. Fertilisers washed from farmland into rivers feed the growth of seaweed, which competes with coral for space. Destructive fishing methods, including the use of explosives, break up the fragile limestone structures that take centuries to form. Furthermore, as the oceans absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, they become more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Conservationists have responded with a range of measures. In some regions, fishing has been banned in protected zones, and populations of fish that eat seaweed have recovered, helping the reefs to regrow. Other teams grow corals in underwater nurseries and attach the fragments to damaged reefs; more than 100,000 pieces have been planted in one such programme. Scientists are also breeding heat-resistant varieties, which they hope will survive in warmer water.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These efforts are valuable, but most researchers agree that they cannot succeed without a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. Estimates suggest that if global temperatures rise by 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, up to 99 per cent of the world's reefs could be lost, compared with 70 to 90 per cent at 1.5 degrees. In other words, a difference of half a degree might determine whether any significant reefs survive.

6.title: Renewable Energy and the Electricity Grid

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Renewable sources supplied roughly 30 per cent of the world's electricity in the early 2020s, up from about 20 per cent two decades earlier, and the cost of solar power fell by around 90 per cent over the same period. The share was 20 per cent in 2002, 21 per cent in 2008, 23 per cent in 2014, 28 per cent in 2018 and 30 per cent in 2022. Governments that once subsidised wind and solar farms to make them competitive now find that, in many regions, they are the cheapest way to generate new electricity. Yet this success has exposed a problem that is technical rather than financial.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Unlike coal or gas plants, wind turbines and solar panels cannot be switched on at will. Output depends on the weather, and it may peak at times when demand is low. On a sunny spring afternoon, some grids produce more electricity than can be used, and operators are forced to pay industrial customers to consume it or simply to shut down generators. Conversely, during a windless winter evening, supply may fall short just as households switch on lights and heaters. Maintaining a stable supply under such conditions requires a degree of flexibility that older networks were not designed to provide.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Several solutions are being pursued simultaneously. Large batteries can store surplus energy for a few hours, and installations of this kind have grown rapidly; capacity in one country doubled within two years. Hydroelectric reservoirs can be used in a similar way, with water pumped uphill when electricity is cheap and released through turbines when it is scarce. Longer storage, which is necessary to cover weeks of poor weather, remains much more expensive, and technologies such as hydrogen are still at an early stage.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Another approach is to manage demand. Smart meters allow tariffs to vary during the day, so that households are encouraged to run washing machines or charge electric cars when power is plentiful. Trials in several cities showed that peak demand could be reduced by up to 15 per cent without noticeable inconvenience. A third option is to expand the transmission network, since wind may be blowing in one region while the sky is overcast in another. However, new power lines often take more than a decade to be approved and built, and local residents sometimes oppose them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In practice, no single measure will be sufficient. Energy analysts expect that future systems will combine several of them, along with a smaller contribution from flexible gas or nuclear plants that can fill remaining gaps. The challenge, they say, is no longer to produce clean electricity but to deliver it reliably, which will demand investment, planning and public acceptance as much as engineering skill.

6.title: Deforestation and the Price of Land

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Forests currently cover about 31 per cent of the world's land area, but each year an estimated ten million hectares are lost, an area roughly the size of Iceland. The majority of this clearance takes place in the tropics, where land is converted to cattle pasture, soybean fields and palm oil plantations. Because trees store carbon, the felling and burning of forests is thought to account for around a tenth of global greenhouse gas emissions.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Explanations for deforestation have traditionally emphasised poverty: small-scale farmers, it was argued, clear land simply to survive. More recent research, however, suggests that commercial agriculture is responsible for a much larger share of forest loss than subsistence farming. Satellite monitoring has made it possible to trace specific areas of cleared forest to particular commodities, and these data have revealed that a small number of products, notably beef and soybeans, are responsible for a disproportionate share of the damage. Consumers in distant countries are therefore implicated, even if they are unaware of it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Governments and companies have introduced various remedies. Some countries have enforced stricter penalties for illegal logging and have designated indigenous territories, which tend to experience far lower rates of clearance than comparable unprotected land. Several major retailers have pledged to purchase only commodities that have been certified as deforestation free. Yet these promises have often proved difficult to verify, since supply chains pass through numerous intermediaries and animals may be raised on one farm before being moved to another.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Economists have proposed a different strategy: paying countries or communities to keep their forests intact. Under such arrangements, which are known as payments for ecosystem services, money is transferred from wealthier governments or companies seeking to offset their emissions to those who protect trees. One large programme was credited with reducing clearance by roughly a third over a decade. In that programme, annual clearance fell from 30,000 hectares in the first year to 28,000 in year three, 24,000 in year five, 21,000 in year seven and 20,000 in year ten. Critics argue that such payments can be wasted if monitoring is weak or if deforestation simply moves to an unprotected area, a phenomenon known as leakage.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Ultimately, the fate of the world's forests is likely to depend on whether the value of standing trees can be made to exceed the value of the land when cleared. Achieving this will probably require a combination of enforcement, transparent supply chains and financial incentives, together with sustained pressure from consumers. None of these measures, taken separately, appears sufficient, but together they offer reasons for cautious optimism.

7.title: Is an Underground Railway Worth the Price?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Underground railways are among the most expensive pieces of infrastructure a city can build. Digging tunnels beneath existing streets and buildings is far more difficult than laying track at ground level, and a kilometre of metro line in a dense city centre can cost up to ten times as much as a kilometre of surface tramway. Even so, dozens of cities have opened new metro systems over the past thirty years, and many more are planning them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Supporters point out that no other form of urban transport can move so many people so quickly. A single metro line can carry up to 40,000 passengers per hour in each direction, which is several times the capacity of a motorway lane. Because trains run beneath the surface, they are not slowed by congestion, so journey times are more predictable than those of buses or cars. In addition, studies in several cities have found that homes within walking distance of a station are worth between 5 and 15 per cent more than similar homes further away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics, however, focus on the financial risks. An international review of rail projects found that the final bill was on average 40 per cent higher than the original estimate, and that passenger numbers were frequently lower than predicted. When ticket sales fail to cover running costs, the shortfall must be paid by taxpayers, including those who rarely use the system. Construction can also last for a decade or more, and the noise and disruption damage local businesses along the route.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A growing number of planners therefore recommend cheaper alternatives. Bus rapid transit, in which buses run in dedicated lanes separated from other traffic, can be built in a fraction of the time and at roughly one tenth of the cost of a metro. Such systems carry fewer passengers than trains, but in cities of moderate size they often provide the most practical solution. Bogotá's TransMilenio, one of the best-known examples, has been copied in cities on several continents.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Most experts agree that there is no single correct answer. A metro is easiest to justify where population density is high, roads are already overcrowded and the city can afford the long-term costs. In smaller or more spread-out cities, a well-designed bus network may deliver greater benefits per dollar spent. The most successful transport policies, it seems, are those that match the technology to the size and shape of the city rather than to its ambitions.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Congestion charging, the practice of making motorists pay to enter a defined area of a city, was once considered politically impossible. Elected officials feared that drivers would be furious, and for decades the idea remained largely theoretical. Road space is a scarce resource, yet in most cities it is offered free at the point of use, so drivers have no incentive to consider the delay their presence imposes on others. 8.title: News in the Age of Algorithms

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until recently, the news that citizens encountered was selected by editors, whose decisions about what mattered shaped public debate. Today, a growing proportion of people, particularly those under 35, receive news mainly through social media platforms, where the selection is made by algorithms designed to maximise the time users spend on the site. This shift, which has taken place within little more than a decade, has prompted researchers to ask what effect it has on the quality of public knowledge.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A study conducted across six countries found that people who relied mainly on social media for news could name, on average, fewer than half as many current political events as those who followed newspapers or broadcast news. Interestingly, however, the social media group reported feeling just as well informed. The authors describe this gap between actual knowledge and perceived knowledge as the 'illusion of awareness', and they argue that it is the feature of the new system which poses the greatest risk to democratic participation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One explanation that has attracted considerable attention is the so-called filter bubble: the idea that algorithms, which learn from what users click on, show them more of what they already believe. Critics claim that this deepens political division. The evidence, though, is less conclusive than is often assumed. Several large studies have found that the majority of users, whose online habits are in fact quite varied, still encounter opinions they disagree with. The researchers suggest that personal choice, such as the decision whom to follow, may matter more than the algorithm.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second concern is the economic damage to news organisations, whose advertising revenue has fallen sharply as companies have moved their budgets to online platforms. Between 2005 and 2020, the number of journalists employed by local newspapers in the country studied fell by almost a third. Where local reporting disappears, researchers have observed lower voter turnout and a decline in scrutiny of local officials, although they acknowledge that other factors may also contribute.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some platforms have responded by labelling disputed content or by reducing the visibility of posts that fact-checkers have judged to be false. Evaluations of these measures have produced mixed results. Labels appear to reduce the sharing of false stories, yet they may also cause readers to treat unlabelled stories, which have not necessarily been checked, as reliable. Education offers an alternative: pupils who are taught to evaluate sources in school perform considerably better in tests of news literacy than those who are not.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Few researchers believe that the solution lies in abandoning social media, which many people value for reasons that have nothing to do with news. Instead, most advocate a combination of clearer platform policies, sustainable funding for independent journalism and better media education. Taken together, such measures might help users to become more discerning readers, rather than merely more frequent ones.

paragraphs.text: When Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, it buried the Roman town of Pompeii under several metres of ash and pumice. The disaster was a tragedy for the inhabitants, but it has given modern archaeologists an unusually detailed picture of everyday life, because buildings, tools and even food were sealed in place. Among the most revealing discoveries are the town's bakeries. Excavators have identified more than thirty of them, which suggests that bread was central to the diet of a population estimated at around 12,000 people.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A typical Pompeian bakery combined several functions under one roof. Grain was ground in large mills made of volcanic stone, each turned by a donkey or by enslaved workers walking in circles. The flour was then mixed with water and a little old dough, shaped into round loaves, and baked in a domed brick oven that closely resembles the pizza ovens still used in Italy today. Many bakeries also had a shop front opening onto the street, so that customers could buy bread directly from the people who had made it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In one oven, excavators found more than eighty loaves that had been turned to charcoal by the heat of the eruption. Several of them were stamped with a name, which historians believe may have identified the baker or the owner of the business. Because carbonised bread keeps its shape for centuries, such finds allow researchers to measure the size of ancient loaves and to study the grains that were used. Most flour was made from wheat, although barley was also common. In one survey of carbonised grain recovered from the bakeries, about 70 per cent of the samples were wheat, 20 per cent were barley and 10 per cent came from other grains.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The diet of the town can also be read from the bodies of its people. Researchers who have examined skeletons from the region report that many adults had badly worn teeth, which they attribute partly to the fine grit left in stone-ground flour. Some argue that the real number of working businesses was considerably lower than thirty, while others believe that baking at home was rare and that the town depended on its professional bakers.

9.title: The Box That Shrank the World

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Before the 1950s, moving goods by sea was slow, expensive and unpredictable. Cargo arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels and crates, and dockworkers unloaded each item by hand or with simple cranes. A ship could spend as long in port as it did at sea, and a significant share of goods was damaged or stolen before it reached its destination.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The solution came from an American trucking entrepreneur, Malcolm McLean, who realised that the real problem was not the ship but the handling of cargo. In April 1956 he sent fifty-eight metal containers from Newark to Houston aboard a converted tanker, the Ideal X. Because the containers were of a standard size, they could be lifted straight from a lorry onto a ship, and later from a ship onto a train, without anyone opening them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The savings were dramatic. According to figures often quoted by economic historians, the cost of loading a ton of cargo fell from nearly six dollars to roughly sixteen cents within about ten years. Ships also spent far less time in port, with turnaround measured in hours rather than days. Goods suffered less damage and theft, which in turn reduced insurance costs. In one commonly cited series, the cost of loading a ton was about 5.86 dollars in 1956, 2.50 dollars in 1960, 0.70 dollars in 1964 and 0.16 dollars in 1966.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Adoption, however, was not immediate. Dockworkers' unions feared for their jobs, and with good reason: ports that once employed thousands of people now needed only a few crane operators. Standardisation also took years, because shipping companies and railways initially used boxes of different sizes. It was only when international agreement on common dimensions was reached in the late 1960s, and when the Vietnam War created huge military demand for efficient supply lines, that the system began to operate on a global scale.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Many economists now argue that the container has done more to increase international trade than any trade agreement. Cheap shipping allowed manufacturers to build factories far from their customers, so that a product might be designed in one country, assembled in another and sold in a third. 9.title: Sleep and the Making of Memories

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For centuries, sleep was regarded as a passive state in which the brain simply rests. Research since the 1950s, when scientists first identified rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, has overturned this view. During a night the brain moves through several stages, completing a full cycle roughly every ninety minutes, and each stage appears to serve a different purpose.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Slow-wave sleep, the deepest stage, seems particularly important for consolidating factual memories. In a widely used type of experiment, volunteers learn a list of word pairs in the evening. Those who are allowed to sleep afterwards typically recall noticeably more pairs the next morning than those kept awake for the same period. Brain imaging suggests that, during slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus, which stores new information temporarily, repeatedly replays the day's activity to the cortex, where it is retained for the long term.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: REM sleep, in which most vivid dreaming occurs, has been linked to emotional memory and to creative thinking. In one well-known experiment, participants who had entered REM sleep during an afternoon nap performed better on word puzzles requiring unusual connections than participants who had rested without sleeping. The researchers suggested that the dreaming brain is able to combine ideas that are normally kept apart.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The practical implications for students are considerable. Surveys indicate that many university students sleep fewer than seven hours on weekdays. In one such survey, 18 per cent of students reported sleeping fewer than six hours, 32 per cent six to seven hours, 38 per cent seven to eight hours and 12 per cent more than eight hours. A number of them regularly stay awake all night before an examination. Researchers argue that this strategy is counterproductive, since information crammed into the evening may never be properly consolidated. Some schools that have moved the start of the school day later report better attendance and improved concentration, although the evidence for higher grades is not conclusive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not all scientists agree about how sleep affects memory. Some argue that the benefit is simply a matter of reduced interference, because a sleeping brain receives no new input that could overwrite what has just been learned. Others maintain that sleep actively strengthens neural connections. The size of the effect also varies between individuals, and older adults appear to gain less from sleep than young people do. For this reason, researchers caution against claiming that extra sleep will automatically improve exam results.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all marine species. Reefs also protect coastlines from storm waves and support the fisheries and tourism that provide an income for hundreds of millions of people. Their decline is therefore a concern far beyond the scientific community.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Corals are animals, but most reef-building species depend on microscopic algae that live inside their tissue. The algae use sunlight to produce food and, in exchange, receive shelter and nutrients; they also give the coral its colour. When seawater becomes unusually warm, this partnership breaks down and the coral expels the algae, turning white. This process is known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not yet dead, but it is starving, and if high temperatures last for several weeks it often dies.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Mass bleaching was rare before the 1980s, but it has since become far more frequent. Major global events have been recorded in 1998, in 2010 and between 2014 and 2017. On Australia's Great Barrier Reef, consecutive bleaching in 2016 and 2017 was so severe that researchers estimated that roughly half of the shallow-water corals were lost. Surveys of the northern reef recorded average live coral cover of about 28 per cent in 2015, 22 per cent in 2016, 13 per cent in 2017 and 12 per cent in 2018. Because corals need years to regrow, the intervals between such events are now often too short for full recovery.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Warming is not the only threat. Run-off containing fertiliser feeds algae that smother corals, overfishing removes the grazing fish that keep those algae in check, and the absorption of carbon dioxide by the sea makes the water more acidic, so that corals find it harder to build their skeletons. Scientists stress that local protection can still make a difference: reefs inside well-managed marine protected areas, where fishing is restricted, tend to recover faster after bleaching than reefs outside them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Several restoration methods are being tried. In so-called coral gardening, fragments are grown in underwater nurseries and then attached to damaged reefs, while some laboratories are breeding corals that tolerate higher temperatures. Critics argue that these projects are expensive and cover tiny areas compared with the size of the ocean. Most researchers agree that restoration can buy time but cannot replace the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions.

10.title: Nudging Behaviour: The Economics of Default Options

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Traditional economic theory assumes that individuals are rational agents who weigh costs and benefits carefully and act in their own long-term interest. Since the 1970s, however, psychologists such as Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky have documented systematic departures from this ideal. People give more weight to losses than to equivalent gains, put off unpleasant decisions, and tend to follow the path of least resistance. The field that has grown out of these observations is known as behavioural economics.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of its most influential ideas is the "nudge", popularised in a 2008 book by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein. A nudge is a change in the way choices are presented that alters behaviour in a predictable way, without forbidding any option or significantly changing economic incentives. Arguably the most powerful nudge is the default option, the outcome that occurs if the individual does nothing. Because inertia is so strong, defaults tend to be accepted by a large majority of people, regardless of whether they were designed to serve those people's interests.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Organ donation illustrates the effect. In some European countries where citizens must actively register as donors, only a small minority, in certain cases fewer than fifteen per cent, have done so. In neighbouring countries where consent is presumed unless a person chooses to opt out, participation exceeds ninety per cent. Yet higher consent rates do not translate directly into more transplants, since the number of organs actually available also depends on hospital procedures, the way in which families are approached and the number of suitable donors.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A similar pattern has been observed in pension saving. In the United Kingdom, a policy of automatic enrolment introduced in 2012 required employers to place eligible employees in a workplace pension scheme, although employees remained free to leave it. According to government figures, participation among eligible private-sector employees rose from just over forty per cent to almost ninety per cent in roughly six years. The published figures show participation of 42 per cent in 2012, 54 per cent in 2014, 77 per cent in 2016 and 88 per cent in 2018. Notably, the large majority of those enrolled stayed in the scheme, even though they could have withdrawn at any time.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Critics raise several objections. Some philosophers argue that nudges are manipulative because they exploit cognitive weaknesses and work below the level of conscious awareness, and they ask who has the authority to decide what counts as a "good" outcome. Others point out that the evidence for effectiveness is uneven: a review of large-scale trials run by government nudge units found average effects considerably smaller than those reported in the original academic studies, possibly because journals prefer to publish successes. Supporters reply that even modest effects are valuable when the cost of an intervention is low, and that choices must always be presented in some way, so that a perfectly neutral design does not exist.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The same techniques are widely used in commerce, often with less benevolent aims. Online retailers have long added optional insurance or subscriptions to a customer's basket by means of pre-ticked boxes, and in the European Union such practices were restricted by consumer legislation in 2011. The episode shows that the real question is not whether choices will be shaped, but by whom, and in whose interest.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the nineteenth century, archaeologists could say that one object was older than another, but they could rarely say by how much. Relative sequences were built from the layers of soil, or strata, in which artefacts were found: the deeper the layer, the earlier the object. Absolute dates depended on written records, which exist for only a tiny fraction of human history. This changed in the late 1940s, when the chemist Willard Libby announced a method of measuring age directly from the remains of living things.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Radiocarbon dating rests on a simple principle. All living organisms absorb carbon, including a small proportion of the radioactive isotope carbon-14, which is created in the upper atmosphere by cosmic rays. When an organism dies it stops absorbing carbon, and the carbon-14 already present decays at a known rate, halving roughly every 5,730 years: about 50 per cent remains after 5,730 years, 25 per cent after 11,460 years, 12.5 per cent after 17,190 years and 6 per cent after 22,920 years. By measuring how much remains in a sample of wood, bone or charcoal, scientists can calculate when the organism died. Because the quantity falls to negligible levels after about 50,000 years, the technique cannot be applied to older material.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Early practitioners assumed that the level of carbon-14 in the atmosphere had been constant through time, but this proved incorrect. Comparisons with tree rings, which can be counted year by year in long-lived trees, showed that radiocarbon years diverge from calendar years, in some periods by several centuries. Researchers therefore developed calibration curves that convert one into the other. Results are normally published with a margin of error, for example 3,200 plus or minus 40 years, which reminds readers that a radiocarbon date is a statistical estimate rather than an exact figure.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Radiocarbon dating is not suitable for every kind of find. Stone tools and most pottery contain no organic carbon, so other techniques are needed. Luminescence dating measures the energy that has accumulated in minerals since they were last heated or exposed to sunlight, and it has been used to date pottery and sediments hundreds of thousands of years old. For still older sites in East Africa, geologists have applied potassium-argon dating to layers of volcanic ash above and below fossil-bearing deposits, allowing them to establish the age of early hominin remains at nearly two million years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The accuracy of any method depends heavily on the quality of the sample. Contamination by modern carbon, for example from handling with bare hands or from preservatives applied to museum specimens, can make an old sample appear younger; as little as one per cent of modern carbon can make a 40,000-year-old sample seem several thousand years younger. Laboratories therefore clean samples carefully before measurement. Even a perfect result may mislead, however. Charcoal from a timber beam, for instance, may come from a tree that was already centuries old when it was felled and burnt. For this reason, archaeologists stress that dates must be combined with several lines of independent evidence before conclusions are drawn.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Recent advances have widened the range of what can be dated. Accelerator mass spectrometry counts individual carbon atoms and needs only a few milligrams of material, so researchers can test a single seed or a tiny fragment of parchment instead of sacrificing a large object. This has encouraged museums to allow sampling of precious items, and it has occasionally produced results that forced historians to revise long-held assumptions about when a particular object was made.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until the early nineteenth century, lighthouses were remarkably inefficient. Most relied on open coal fires or oil lamps placed in front of simple metal reflectors, and the light they produced was weak, uneven and easily lost in fog. This mattered more every year, because the growth of maritime trade meant that increasing numbers of vessels were passing hazardous coasts, and a great many of them were wrecked on rocks that a better warning light might have revealed. Attempts to improve matters with larger lamps merely produced more smoke and heat, and the fundamental problem, that most of the light escaped in all directions rather than out to sea, remained unsolved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In 1819 the French lighthouse commission asked Augustin-Jean Fresnel, a young civil engineer who was already known for his research on the wave theory of light, to examine the problem. Fresnel's insight was that a single thick lens, which absorbs much of the light passing through it and is extremely heavy, was the wrong solution. Instead, he built a lens from a series of concentric rings of glass prisms, each ring angled so that it bent the light into one horizontal beam. The design used far less glass, which meant that a lens could be very large while remaining transparent. It was first installed at the Cordouan lighthouse in 1823, and sailors reported that its light could be seen from a much greater distance than before. According to one contemporary estimate, a coal fire could be seen from about 10 kilometres, a reflector lamp from about 15 kilometres and a Fresnel lens from about 30 kilometres.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Adoption was uneven. Britain and France converted their main lights within a few decades, but the United States moved slowly. The official in charge of American lighthouses until 1852 preferred cheaper reflector systems and resisted pressure to change. It was only after a government inquiry criticised the service, and a new board took control, that Fresnel lenses were widely installed in the 1850s. The delay is often cited as an example of how administrative thrift can undermine safety.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The largest lenses, known as first-order lenses, stood more than two metres high and contained hundreds of prisms. To make such a heavy structure turn, many lighthouses floated the lens on a bath of mercury, so that a small clockwork mechanism driven by a falling weight could rotate it. Each lighthouse was also given a distinctive flash pattern, allowing navigators to identify their position by counting the interval between flashes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Electricity, automation and, more recently, satellite navigation have reduced the importance of lighthouses, and most are now unmanned. Yet Fresnel's principle has survived. Variations of his thin, light lens appear in car headlamps, overhead projectors and devices that concentrate sunlight. Some maritime authorities also argue that lighthouses remain a valuable back-up if satellite signals are jammed or fail, which is why many continue to operate.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The keepers who tended these lights led demanding lives. On isolated rock stations, relief crews could be delayed for weeks by storms, and the keepers had to polish the prisms every day, wind the clockwork and record the weather throughout the night. Their logbooks, many of which survive, have since become valuable sources for historians of climate and maritime life.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Within roughly three years of birth, children in almost every society master the basic grammar of their native language without any formal teaching. A task that challenges adult learners for years is accomplished by toddlers who cannot yet tie their shoelaces. Explaining how this happens has been a central goal of psychology and linguistics for more than half a century, and the debate has often been framed as a contest between nature and nurture.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In the 1950s, Noam Chomsky argued that the speech children hear is too limited and too full of errors to explain what they learn, so they must be born with innate knowledge of the basic structure of language. Other researchers respond that infants are powerful statistical learners. In a well-known experiment published in 1996, Jenny Saffran and her colleagues played eight-month-old babies a continuous stream of made-up syllables for just two minutes. The babies afterwards responded differently to syllable sequences that had formed "words" and to those that had crossed word boundaries, which suggests that even very young infants keep track of how often sounds occur together.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Another line of research concerns the sounds of speech. At six to eight months, babies raised in English-speaking homes can distinguish sound contrasts that occur only in other languages, such as certain consonants in Hindi. By about twelve months this ability has weakened, whereas sensitivity to the sounds of the native language has become sharper. In one set of tests, babies aged six to eight months picked out a Hindi contrast about 80 per cent of the time, babies aged eight to ten months about 65 per cent and babies aged ten to twelve months about 55 per cent. Psychologists describe this as a narrowing of perception: the brain stops attending to differences that are not useful in the environment it finds itself in.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Patricia Kuhl and her colleagues have shown that mere exposure is not enough. In one study, American nine-month-olds took part in a series of play sessions with a native speaker of Mandarin. Infants who met the speaker in person learned to distinguish Mandarin sounds, but those who watched the same speaker on video, or heard only an audio recording, did not. Kuhl concluded that social engagement, with its eye contact and responsiveness, may switch on the learning mechanism in a way that passive listening cannot.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The role of the home environment is more controversial. A famous study by Betty Hart and Todd Risley reported that, by the age of three, children from professional families had heard around thirty million more words than children from families receiving welfare, a difference linked to later school success. The claim inspired campaigns urging parents to talk to their babies. However, the study involved only forty-two families, and later research has found much smaller gaps. Several critics argue that the quality of conversation, rather than the number of words, is what matters.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Most researchers now accept that these explanations are not mutually exclusive. Statistical learning may help infants to find words in a stream of speech, social interaction may motivate them to pay attention, and innate constraints may limit the kinds of grammar they consider. What remains unresolved is how much of the machinery is specific to language, and how much is simply general learning ability applied to speech.
